tldr: The authors propose Logic-VLA, a vision-language-action (VLA) model that directly takes Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications at inference time to handle strict constraints—like safety distances or time bounds—that natural language instructions struggle to specify. Combining a syntax-graph logic encoder with a two-stage post-training pipeline on top of a pre-trained base model, Logic-VLA boosts requirement satisfaction rates by up to 40.7 percentage points with almost no drop in nominal task success.
hero_caption: Overview of Logic-VLA. On the left, a syntax-graph encoder is pre-trained on an auxiliary task predicting quantitative robustness values from trajectory-STL formula pairs. On the right, its output is prepended to the pre-trained VLA ($\pi_{0.5}$) input tokens, and the policy adapts through two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on satisfying demonstrations, followed by trajectory-level preference optimization (IPO) on matched satisfying-violating rollout pairs.
overview:
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models can guide robots flexibly following natural-language (NL) instructions like "go around the desk." However, NL instructions alone struggle to convey precise spatiotemporal constraints or safety requirements unambiguously, such as "always stay at least 50 cm away from the desk" or "pass through this area within 10 seconds." Retraining a brand-new control policy every time a constraint changes is simply impractical.

To address this, the authors introduce Logic-VLA, a model that accepts Signal Temporal Logic (STL)—a formal language capable of strictly specifying spatiotemporal requirements on trajectories—as an additional input at inference time. The core idea is to encode the STL syntax tree using a Graph Neural Network (GNN) and embed it directly into the VLA token space. Furthermore, they establish a two-stage post-training framework: supervised fine-tuning on constraint-satisfying demonstrations (Stage 1), followed by preference optimization (Stage 2) using matched pairs of satisfying and violating trajectories on the same task.

Evaluated on closed-loop quadcopter warehouse navigation in the NVIDIA Isaac Sim physics simulator, Logic-VLA improved STL satisfaction rates by 24.8 to 40.7 percentage points over an STL-blind baseline, while reducing the nominal NL task success rate by at most 1.8 pp. It also showed strong generalization to unseen formulas and parameters, proving that a single VLA can flexibly adapt to diverse formal requirements on the fly.
contributions: Proposed Logic-VLA, a VLA architecture conditioned on arbitrary Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications at inference time, executing them alongside natural-language task instructions.
Developed an STL logic encoder combining syntax-graph representations and robustness-semantics pre-training to capture the structure of predicates, time intervals, and logical operators.

Constructed a two-stage post-training framework combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on satisfying demonstrations with flow-matching-adapted Identity Preference Optimization (IPO) on matched satisfying-violating pairs.

Demonstrated in Isaac Sim closed-loop quadcopter navigation experiments that the policy improves requirement satisfaction rates by 24.8 to 40.7 percentage points across multiple benchmarks, including unseen formulas, while preserving nominal language task performance.

sections.heading: Is "Go around the desk" enough? Balancing language instructions and safety constraints
sections.summary: While VLA models excel at following language instructions, they struggle to handle strict requirements like safety margins or deadlines unambiguously. This paper presents Logic-VLA, which accepts Signal Temporal Logic (STL) at inference time to adapt a single model to diverse formal specifications.
sections.details:
VLA models have shown impressive success toward building robots that follow intuitive human instructions. However, natural-language commands are better suited for stating what to do in broad strokes than for specifying exact behaviors—such as staying a precise distance away from obstacles or visiting waypoints in a strict order and within exact deadlines.

In robotics, Signal Temporal Logic (STL) has been widely used to express and evaluate such trajectory-level spatiotemporal constraints. Yet integrating formal specifications like STL into existing VLAs has typically required either training separate policies for every new constraint or sacrificing the original natural-language task-following capabilities.

To overcome this, the authors propose a post-training framework that allows a pre-trained VLA to dynamically take STL specifications as additional inputs at inference time. Building upon the pre-trained $\pi_{0.5}$ base model, they attach a syntax-graph encoder for STL formulas and combine imitation learning on satisfying demonstrations with preference optimization. This setup enforces safety and spatiotemporal constraints without compromising nominal language task execution.

sections.heading: VLAs, post-training, and temporal logic: At the intersection of three fields
sections.summary: The authors review related work across three areas: safety-aware VLA learning, reinforcement learning and preference-based post-training for VLAs, and robot trajectory planning and learning with STL. Unlike methods that align a policy to a fixed global reward, this work uniquely treats the runtime logical formula itself as a policy input.
sections.details:
This work connects three main research domains:

- **Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models and Safety**: While VLAs show strong generalization in manipulation and navigation, language alone cannot precisely pin down execution margins. Prior efforts have introduced post-hoc filters using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) or Model Predictive Control (MPC), or used temporal logic in discrete high-level planning. In contrast, this paper pursues an end-to-end approach where the VLA policy itself takes temporal logic as an input and generates actions directly.

- **VLA Post-training**: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone struggles to distinguish subtle differences between good and bad actions on the same task. As a result, preference optimization techniques like DPO and IPO are increasingly applied to robot policies. While existing approaches align the entire policy toward a single fixed objective (like global safety), this work provides the desired behavior (the STL specification) as an input, allowing the model to adapt to different requirements across deployment scenarios.

- **Planning and Learning with Signal Temporal Logic (STL)**: STL features quantitative robustness semantics that measure how well a trajectory satisfies a specification, which has been leveraged in optimization-based trajectory generation and generative model conditioning. However, most prior visual STL works were restricted to open-loop trajectory generation. Integrating STL directly into a closed-loop VLA that interleaves observation and action is a new step forward.

sections.heading: The basics of robot control setup and Signal Temporal Logic (STL)
sections.summary: This section formalizes the problem of generating actions in a closed loop from observations, language, and logic formulas, and reviews core STL syntax and robustness semantics. The objective is to build a single policy that satisfies arbitrary runtime STL specifications without degrading nominal natural-language task performance.
sections.details:
### Robot Control Setup
Consider a discrete-time system where a VLA policy $\pi_\theta$ receives an observation $o_{t_d}$ and a natural-language instruction $l$ at each decision step $t_d$, outputting an action chunk of $K_a$ steps. As the robot tracks these actions and interacts with the environment, it produces a state trajectory $s = (s_0, s_1, \dots, s_H)$. The goal of this work is to post-train an adapted policy $\pi_{\tilde{\theta}}(\cdot \mid o, l, \phi)$ that simultaneously satisfies an additional STL specification $\phi$ supplied at inference time.

### Overview of Signal Temporal Logic (STL)
STL is a formal specification language used to describe desired properties over continuous-time signal sequences. It consists of predicates $\pi^\mu$ (e.g., keeping obstacle clearance above a threshold $\mu(s_t) \geq 0$), negation $\neg$, conjunction $\wedge$, and temporal operators such as the interval-bounded Until operator $U_{[a,b]}$. From these, useful operators like Eventually ($F_{[a,b]}\phi$) and Globally ($G_{[a,b]}\phi$) are derived.

A key strength of STL is its **robustness semantics** $\rho^\phi(s)$, which outputs a real-valued score indicating not just satisfaction (True/False), but how safely the trajectory satisfies or violates the requirement. A positive value denotes satisfaction and a negative value denotes violation, with larger positive numbers reflecting greater safety margins.

### Challenges to Address
This problem presents three primary hurdles. First, post-training must not degrade the policy's nominal language task capabilities. Second, learning to correctly interpret complex STL syntax purely through SFT is difficult. Third, because STL is evaluated globally over the entire trajectory, it cannot be straightforwardly decomposed into step-by-step action-chunk losses.

sections.heading: Tokenizing formulas and learning from good vs. bad rollouts: A two-stage recipe
sections.summary: Logic-VLA combines an STL syntax-graph GNN encoder with a two-stage post-training pipeline. The encoder is first pre-trained on robustness prediction, followed by imitation learning on satisfying demonstrations (Stage 1) and flow-matching-adapted IPO preference optimization on matched satisfying-violating pairs (Stage 2).
sections.details:
### IV-A Constructing Logic-Conditioned Training Data
First, the authors collect an in-domain trajectory dataset $D$ and define a candidate set of STL formulas $\Phi$. Using an offline monitoring tool based on quantitative robustness semantics, each trajectory is labeled as satisfying or violating each formula. From this, they automatically build a satisfying demonstration set $D^+$ and a preference dataset $P$ containing matched pairs of one satisfying and one violating rollout under identical tasks and environments.

### IV-B Logic Encoder Architecture and Pre-training
To translate an STL formula $\phi$ into a representation the VLA can process, the authors adopt a syntax-graph encoder based on TeLoGraF. Operators and predicate nodes (signal types, thresholds, inequality directions) serve as node features, aggregated into a fixed-length vector via a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN).

Crucially, **the encoder is pre-trained**. Paired with a trajectory encoder, it is trained on an auxiliary regression task to predict how well a given trajectory satisfies the formula (the robustness value $\rho$). This imbues the encoder with an understanding of time intervals, thresholds, and logical structures. After pre-training, the resulting vector is linearly projected into multiple specification tokens $Z_\phi$ and appended to the visual and language token sequence fed into the VLA.

### IV-C Two-Stage Post-Training
Using the flow-matching-based $\pi_{0.5}$ as the backbone, fine-tuning proceeds in two stages:

- **Stage 1 (STL-conditioned SFT)**: Imitation learning is run strictly on the satisfying demonstration dataset $D^+$ using standard flow-matching loss. This teaches the base model the baseline behavior of conditioning on logic tokens.
- **Stage 2 (Trajectory-Level Preference Optimization)**: The model is trained on preference pairs $P$ consisting of satisfying rollouts $p_i^+$ and violating rollouts $p_i^-$. Because exact likelihood ratios are computationally expensive in flow matching, the authors use the difference in flow-matching losses as a surrogate for the log-probability ratio, averaging losses across multiple time windows to compute a global trajectory score. The objective adapts margin-based Identity Preference Optimization (IPO) to prevent over-optimization, augmented with a one-sided anchor term that prevents fitting degradation on satisfying demonstrations relative to the reference policy.

sections.heading: Drone navigation in Isaac Sim: Can it follow unseen logic formulas?
sections.summary: Evaluated on quadcopter navigation in a photorealistic warehouse simulator, Logic-VLA improved STL satisfaction rates by 24.8 to 40.7 percentage points while keeping the nominal language task drop within 1.8 pp, showing strong generalization to unseen formulas.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.1 using a simulated DJI Mavic 2 Pro drone under closed-loop control (predicting and executing 40 actions at 10 Hz). The setup features 6 tasks requiring the drone to visit warehouse landmarks in sequence. STL formulas constraining 3D position $(x, y, z)$ were generated from 90 formula templates combining temporal operators and boolean connectives.

Evaluations covered three difficulty splits:
- **Seen**: Formulas included in training (60 formulas)
- **Unseen Parameter**: Formulas sharing seen structures but with unseen thresholds and time windows (99 formulas)
- **Unseen Structure**: Completely new formula templates never seen during training or encoder pre-training (56 formulas)

### Key Results and Insights
Compared to the logic-blind "Base" policy, Logic-VLA achieved dramatic gains in constraint satisfaction: $+40.7$ pp on Seen, $+26.2$ pp on Unseen Parameter, and $+24.8$ pp on Unseen Structure. Meanwhile, the drop in nominal language task success was minimal, staying within $1.8$ pp at most.

As an alternative baseline, a regularizer directly maximizing smooth robustness semantics was tested. However, increasing its weight to improve satisfaction caused task success to plunge from 68.5% down to 45.0%, as the objective distorted trajectory behaviors excessively. This highlights that preference optimization (IPO) over satisfying-violating pairs is remarkably effective at fixing constraint violations while preserving nominal task execution.

### Ablations
Ablation studies highlighted two key design choices:
- **Impact of Robustness Pre-training**: Compared to a randomly initialized STL encoder, the pre-trained encoder improved satisfaction from 46.7% to 61.7% on Seen, and from 53.0% to 59.5% on Unseen Parameter.
- **Syntax Graphs vs. Text Prompts**: Appending the STL formula as plain text in the language prompt provided some gains, but Logic-VLA's syntax-graph input outperformed it by $+15.5$ pp on Seen satisfaction (82.0% vs. 66.5%) and $+4.7$ pp on Unseen Parameter, confirming the value of explicitly encoding logic structures.

sections.heading: The future of robot control: Merging formal methods with foundation models
sections.summary: The paper presents Logic-VLA, demonstrating that formal specification languages can serve as effective conditioning signals to enhance the controllability of robotic foundation models alongside natural language instructions.
sections.details:
This work introduced Logic-VLA, a temporal-logic-conditioned VLA model. By combining a semantics-pre-trained syntax-graph encoder with a two-stage post-training framework (satisfying-demonstration SFT followed by matched-pair IPO), the model successfully adapts to strict formal specifications while maintaining its nominal natural-language task execution.

Closed-loop drone flight evaluations verified that a single VLA model can dynamically adjust its actions to varied safety and spatiotemporal requirements specified at runtime. By bridging the cognitive generalization of large foundation models with the precision of formal methods, this approach offers valuable foundations for developing dependable autonomous robots.

takeaways: Dividing roles—using natural language for "what to do" and STL (Signal Temporal Logic) for "how to do it safely and precisely"—is a promising path for practical, safe VLA deployments.
Representing formulas as syntax graphs (via GNNs) pre-trained on robustness prediction yields significantly better policy conditioning than simply passing them as plain-text prompts.

Directly optimizing trajectory robustness as a smooth penalty often disrupts nominal task behavior; preference optimization (IPO) over matched satisfying vs. violating rollouts is key to fixing violations without breaking task success.
limitations: Experimental evaluations are currently limited to quadcopter navigation inside a simulator (Isaac Sim); validating on real hardware drones and manipulation setups remains future work.
The approach assumes nominal language tasks and STL specifications are compatible; it lacks mechanisms to resolve or prioritize objectives when tasks and constraints fundamentally conflict.
STL predicates rely on a predefined signal vocabulary (e.g., 3D positions), meaning the model cannot define arbitrary novel geometric or dynamical relations zero-shot.
